fields.definition: A timbral descriptor for sound with reduced high-frequency energy and a relative emphasis on low and low-mid frequencies, giving a subdued, mellow, or closed tonal character.
fields.plain_english: A dark sound has few high notes and more low ones. It sounds soft and warm, a bit like music heard through a closed door.
fields.purpose_function: Provides a shared shorthand for tonal balance so engineers can quickly agree that a source or mix leans toward the low end and lacks treble.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may call a mic or mix dark and then add high-frequency EQ or choose a brighter mic to open it up.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'dark' with 'dull' — dark describes a mellow tonal balance while dull implies missing detail or clarity
Treating dark as a fault when many sources and mixes are meant to sound dark
Trying to fix darkness only by boosting treble instead of checking mic choice, placement, or the source itself
scenario_contexts: A ribbon mic on acoustic guitar sounds too dark, so the engineer tries a condenser or adds high-shelf EQ
A club system is described as dark, prompting a check of high-driver level and system tuning
A producer asks for a darker vocal to suit a moody ballad

fields.definition: Describes sound that lacks a sharp, localizable point of origin and instead seems spread out in space, typically because reverberant or reflected energy dominates the direct sound.
fields.plain_english: A diffuse sound seems to come from all around, not one clear spot. It is like hearing rain, where you cannot point to a single place it comes from.
fields.purpose_function: Lets engineers describe how spread out or unlocalized a sound image is, which matters for imaging, reverb balance, and mic technique.
fields.practical_application: A technician noticing a diffuse, washed-out image may move mics closer to reduce room reflections or lower the reverb send.
common_mistakes: Confusing diffuse (spread-out and unlocalized) with distant (far away but still placeable)
Adding more reverb to a source that is already too diffuse
Miking too far back and blaming the room instead of the distance
scenario_contexts: Room mics on drums sound too diffuse, so the engineer blends in close mics for focus
A choir recording is overly diffuse, prompting closer or tighter mic placement
A reverb setting makes a lead vocal too diffuse to sit forward in the mix

fields.definition: A timbral descriptor for sound containing added distortion, harmonic grit, or noise, giving a rough, aggressive, or gritty character rather than a clean tone.
fields.plain_english: A dirty sound has extra grit or fuzz added to it. It is like a rough, scratchy voice instead of a smooth, clear one.
fields.purpose_function: Gives a quick way to describe intentional or unwanted distortion and added harmonics, guiding choices about gain, saturation, and tone.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may deliberately drive a preamp or amp sim to make a guitar or synth sound dirty, or track down an unwanted dirty tone caused by clipping.
common_mistakes: Confusing an intentional dirty tone with a fault such as accidental clipping or a bad cable
Adding dirt with distortion while ignoring the extra harmonics that can mask other tracks
UNSAFE: cranking amp or monitor gain to chase a dirty tone and reaching harmful listening levels
scenario_contexts: A producer wants a dirty, distorted bass and adds a saturation plugin
A guitarist's DI sounds too clean, so the engineer re-amps it for a dirtier tone
An engineer traces a dirty-sounding vocal to an overdriven mic preamp

fields.definition: Describes a sound that seems far from the listener, typically due to lower level, reduced high-frequency content, weaker transients, and a higher ratio of reverberant to direct sound.
fields.plain_english: A distant sound seems far away from you. Like someone talking from across a big room, it is quieter and less clear than a close sound.
fields.purpose_function: Describes perceived depth and distance, helping engineers manage the front-to-back placement of sources in a mix.
fields.practical_application: To push a backing vocal further back, an engineer adds reverb, rolls off highs, and lowers its level so it sounds more distant.
common_mistakes: Confusing distant (far away) with diffuse (spread out and unlocalized)
Trying to fix an unwantedly distant sound with level alone while ignoring reverb and lost highs
Miking a source too far away, then boosting gain and raising the noise floor
scenario_contexts: A lead vocal sounds distant, so the engineer reduces reverb and adds presence EQ
A producer wants a distant, dreamy backing vocal and pushes it back with reverb
Overhead-only drum mics sound distant, prompting added close mics

fields.definition: Describes a signal with no added reverb, delay, or ambience — the source sound with no spatial effects, though a recording may still capture some of the room it was made in.
fields.plain_english: A dry sound has no echo or reverb added. It is the plain, raw sound by itself, like singing in a small closet full of clothes.
fields.purpose_function: Distinguishes the unprocessed source from a wet, effected signal, which is essential for effect balance, routing, and later re-processing.
fields.practical_application: Engineers often record dry so reverb and delay can be added and adjusted later during the mix.
common_mistakes: Confusing dry (no added effects) with a dead or dull tone
Printing reverb onto a recording instead of keeping a dry track for flexibility
Assuming a dry signal needs no room treatment, when recording still captures room sound
scenario_contexts: A vocal is recorded dry so the mix engineer can choose the reverb later
A guitarist records a dry DI for re-amping
A producer solos the dry signal to check tone before adding effects

fields.definition: A timbral descriptor for sound lacking high-frequency detail, brightness, and clarity, so it seems lifeless, muffled, or short on definition and attack.
fields.plain_english: A dull sound is missing its bright, crisp detail. It sounds muffled and flat, like a cymbal hit with a soft cloth over it.
fields.purpose_function: Flags a lack of clarity and high-frequency detail so engineers know to check the source, mic, or high-frequency EQ.
fields.practical_application: A dull-sounding cymbal track may prompt a brighter mic, better placement, or a high-shelf boost.
common_mistakes: Confusing dull (lacking clarity and detail) with dark (a mellow but still clear tonal balance)
Boosting treble to fix dullness when the real cause is a damaged cable, phase issue, or poor placement
Ignoring a dull monitor sound that is actually a blown tweeter or failing crossover
scenario_contexts: A dull vocal recording leads the engineer to swap to a brighter condenser mic
A PA sounds dull, so the tech checks for a blown high driver
A mastering engineer adds gentle high-shelf EQ to lift a dull mix

fields.definition: A timbral descriptor for sound with harsh, aggressive emphasis in the upper-midrange and high frequencies, producing a hard, biting, or slightly irritating character.
fields.plain_english: An edgy sound is harsh and sharp on the ears. It has a biting, aggressive tone, a bit like a voice that is almost shouting.
fields.purpose_function: Describes unpleasant or aggressive upper-mid energy so engineers know where to tame it, or where to add bite when wanted.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may cut around 2 to 5 kHz to soften an edgy vocal or guitar, or add a little edge for aggression.
common_mistakes: Confusing edgy (aggressive upper-mid tone) with dirty (added distortion)
Cutting all the highs to fix edginess and ending up with a dull sound
Blaming the source when edginess actually comes from a bright room or harsh monitors
scenario_contexts: An edgy vocal gets a narrow cut around 3 kHz to soften it
A distorted guitar sounds edgy, so the engineer rolls off some presence
A producer adds a touch of edge to a synth to help it cut through

fields.definition: A colloquial timbral descriptor for a loose, buzzy, distorted low-frequency sound resembling flatulence, usually caused by driver over-excursion, clipping, or ill-defined bass distortion.
fields.plain_english: A farty sound is a loose, buzzy low note that flaps instead of staying tight. It often comes from a speaker pushed too hard, and sounds a bit like the rude noise its name suggests.
fields.purpose_function: Gives engineers a quick label for a specific loose low-end distortion so they can trace and fix overdriven or ill-defined bass.
fields.practical_application: A farty kick or bass usually signals an overdriven speaker, too much low boost, or clipping, prompting less level or a high-pass filter.
common_mistakes: Assuming farty always means a plugin problem when it is often a physical speaker being over-driven
Boosting low bass further and worsening the loose, farty distortion
UNSAFE: continuing to drive a farty, distorting subwoofer or amp, which can overheat voice coils and damage drivers
scenario_contexts: A subwoofer sounds farty at high level, so the tech engages a high-pass filter and lowers drive
A synth bass patch sounds farty, prompting less distortion or a cleaner sub layer
A bass amp goes farty when pushed, signaling the speaker is near its limit

fields.definition: A timbral descriptor for a full, rich, and weighty sound with strong low-mid content and often subtle harmonic saturation or width, giving a sense of size and body.
fields.plain_english: A fat sound is big, full, and warm. It fills out the low-middle of the sound, making it feel large and rich, like a thick chord instead of a thin one.
fields.purpose_function: Describes a sense of fullness and body so engineers can aim for or dial back weight in a source or mix.
fields.practical_application: To make a thin snare or synth fatter, an engineer may add low-mid EQ, saturation, layering, or slight detuning and doubling.
common_mistakes: Confusing fat (full and rich) with muddy (unclear and boomy)
Adding too much low-mid to fatten a sound and cluttering the mix
Assuming fat only means more bass rather than added body, saturation, and width
scenario_contexts: A thin-sounding synth bass is fattened with saturation and a sub layer
A producer wants a fatter snare and adds low-mid EQ and parallel compression
A vocal is doubled and slightly detuned to sound fatter
